appraisal_events.evidence: Having privately mocked the Cambremers to Morel as no better than 'le dernier pioupiou de son régiment,' Charlus lets Morel snub their invitation (which Morel enacts with burlesque self-importance); when the anxious Cambremers write to Morel to smooth things over, a gesture that 'fit sourire M. de Charlus en lui montrant son pouvoir,' he still fails to appear at the dinner staged in his honor for the impressive Férés, and Mme de Cambremer 'faillit se trouver mal' at the door.
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus's contempt for the Cambremers, first vented privately and enacted through Morel's snub, culminates in his own public no-show at a dinner arranged specifically to showcase him, publicly humiliating Mme de Cambremer before the guests she was most eager to impress.

appraisal_events.evidence: Judging it time to intervene, Mme Verdurin secludes herself with Brichot for an hour, tells him Mme de Cambremer mocks him and that he is the laughingstock of her salon, and shames him with mention of the washerwoman he lives with; she succeeds in ending his visits to Féterne, and his grief is such that for two days it is feared he will go blind, his illness having taken a permanent step forward.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin exercises decisive control over Brichot, deliberately destroying his attachment to Mme de Cambremer and leaving him devastated, a stark demonstration of her authority over her circle.

status_effects.explanation: Charlus's no-show at the dinner staged expressly to display him to the prestigious Férés is a public snub that nearly makes her faint, a humiliation witnessed by the very guests she hoped to impress.
The Cambremers' anxious attempt to placate him through Morel visibly confirms his leverage over them, and his eventual no-show shows he can dictate the terms of the relationship at will.
The narrator frames Morel's literal, self-satisfied enactment of Charlus's aristocratic disdain toward the Cambremers as burlesque, undercutting his affected superiority.
Brichot is manipulated and shamed into abandoning his attachment, left in genuine anguish severe enough to threaten his eyesight, showing him wholly at Mme Verdurin's mercy.
She deliberately and successfully ends Brichot's romantic pursuit through direct intervention, demonstrating full control over a member of her circle.
